intro: Who gets to stand on the mat is decided by rules, laws and governments, not only by coaches. A weight sheet can leave out every woman. A school order can require every boy to take kendo. An army of occupation can close a practice hall. In this unit you will read those rules and the reasons written beside them.

The first chapter follows women and girls into judo, wrestling, taekwondo, fencing and sumo. You will meet a federal law, a medal taken back and a rank limit that lasted decades. The second chapter follows governments in Japan, the Soviet Union and China as they put combat arts into schools and national programs.

By the end, you will be able to explain how a law or an order changed who could compete. You will also compare the reasons governments gave with what else they were doing at the time, using dates as evidence.
bigQuestion: Who decides who may stand on the mat, and what reasons do they give?

timeline.t: The Dai Nippon Butokukai is founded in Kyoto
Mao Zedong's essay on physical education appears in New Youth
Women fence foil at the Paris Olympics
Kendo or judo becomes required for boys in Japanese middle schools
The Soviet Union recognizes sambo as an official sport
The Butokukai is dissolved under the Allied occupation
Title IX is signed; Keiko Fukuda passes the Kodokan's fifth dan limit
The first women's world judo championships are held in New York
Taekwondo enters the Olympics with four classes for women and four for men
Women wrestle for Olympic medals for the first time, in Athens
Budo becomes required again in Japanese junior high schools

test.q: What kind of programs does Title IX cover?
choices: Education programs that receive federal money
test.why: Title IX covers education programs and activities receiving federal money.

test.q: Which sports did the 1975 rules name as contact sports?
test.why: The list included boxing, wrestling, rugby, ice hockey, football and basketball.

test.q: Why did Rusty Kanokogi have to return her 1959 medal?
choices: Officials said women could not enter the contest
test.why: Officials learned she was a woman and said the rules did not allow women.

test.q: When were the first women's world judo championships held?
test.why: Kanokogi organized them at Madison Square Garden in November 1980.

test.q: Who was promoted past the Kodokan's fifth dan limit in 1972?
test.why: The Kodokan promoted Keiko Fukuda to sixth dan in 1972.

test.q: How many women's medal events did boxing hold at its 2012 debut?
test.why: Women's boxing began in London in 2012 with three classes.

test.q: In which sport did women first wrestle for Olympic medals in 2004?
test.why: Women's freestyle wrestling joined the Olympics at Athens in 2004.

test.q: Which fencing weapon did women fence first at the Olympics?
test.why: Women fenced foil at the Olympics from 1924.

test.q: What happened on a sumo ring in Maizuru in 2018?
choices: Women giving first aid were asked to leave
The ring was moved to Tokyo
test.why: When the mayor collapsed, women gave first aid and were told to leave the ring.

test.q: Where did the Butokukai hold its yearly national demonstrations?
test.why: The Butokuden, opened in 1899 in Kyoto, hosted its yearly demonstrations.

test.q: What event in 1931 matched Japan's rule requiring budo for boys?
choices: The end of World War II
test.why: Japan's army seized Manchuria in 1931, the same year budo became required.

test.q: What happened to budo in Japanese schools in late 1945?
choices: It was stopped under occupation orders
It was made required for girls
test.why: The Ministry of Education stopped budo classes following occupation orders.

test.q: When did the All Japan Kendo Federation form?
test.why: The All Japan Kendo Federation was founded in 1952, as the occupation ended.

test.q: Who recognized sambo as an official sport in 1938?
choices: The All-Union Committee for Physical Culture and Sports
test.why: The Soviet All-Union Committee for Physical Culture and Sports recognized sambo.

test.q: What do Japan's 1931 and 2012 school rules have in common?
choices: Both made budo required, but for different stated reasons
Both were written by the occupation
test.why: Both required budo; 1931 spoke of loyalty and spirit, 2012 of culture and respect.

write.prompt: Choose one: a law or rule that opened the mat to women, or a government order that put a martial art into schools. Argue whether it mainly served the athletes or mainly served the goals of the body that wrote it. Cite at least two dated documents or records from this unit, such as Title IX (1972), Japan's 1931 or 2012 school rules, or the Soviet recognition of sambo (1938).
tips: Name each document or record and give its year.
Say who wrote the rule and what else was happening at that time.
Quote or paraphrase the stated reason, then weigh it against the dates.
Use terms from the unit, such as rank ceiling, federation or mobilization.
Compare two cases rather than judging one alone.
